newsitem.title: USA: BOJ seen loath to intervene to stem yen slide.
newsitem.headline: BOJ seen loath to intervene to stem yen slide.

text.p: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) probably prefers to avoid outright market intervention near-term to halt any further depreciation of the yen versus the dollar because the BOJ could get more than it bargained for, U.S. experts said.

By intervening, the Japanese central bank could accomplish its goal of halting the yen's slide, but would also risk setting off an unintended chain reaction which could disrupt the delicate balance of world financial markets.

"In fact, if the Bank of Japan were seen intervening against the dollar, you'd see some pretty dramatic impacts on the financial markets globally, including the U.S. Treasury market," said Tim McGee, chief economist at Tokai Bank.
"So I think that they prefer not to have to start that but rather just use the jawboning for the time being," McGee said.
Japanese officials flooded the market this week with verbal intervention, warning that an excessively weak or strong yen could wreak havoc on Japan's economy.
But despite all the yen-supportive rhetoric, the Japanese currency still traded near 116 per dollar during Wednesday afternoon dealings.

Some officials also vowed Japan will keep close tabs on the market and deal appropriately with excessive movements, prompting speculation about whether the BOJ would really step to the plate if the yen slid further.
The BOJ had joined forces with other central banks to bolster the dollar after it tumbled to a post-World War II low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995.

After other central banks threw in the towel, the BOJ continued supporting the U.S. currency in 1996, helping to pave the way for a rally that swept the dollar to a fresh 45-month high of 117 yen earlier this week.

Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp, said the BOJ may be reluctant to intervene to strengthen the yen as that could send a strong signal to financial markets which might cause the dollar to crash.
The last thing the BOJ wants to do is give the impression the central bank has reversed its foreign exchange policy, said Sohn, a senior vice president.
Indeed Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, reassured the market late last year that Japan's policy had not changed.
Still, the BOJ has plenty of ammunition to defend the yen with reserves at a record level for the 34th consecutive month.

"Clearly, Japan is not going to dump all those dollars on the market, but...I think, the opportunity would be ripe for an over-reaction in the market place (if they did intervene), at least over the short-term," said Michael Faust, a global portfolio manager at Bailard, Biehl and Kaiser.
Reasons may abound for why the BOJ might be disinclined to intervene on behalf of the yen, but some analysts conceded the continuing slump in Tokyo stocks could weaken that resolve.
The key Nikkei 225 index took another nosedive Wednesday, shedding 215.81 points or 1.14 percent to close at 18,680.38, its lowest finish since November 29, 1995.
"If there was a loss of confidence in the yen, then I think they would certainly step in," Tokai's McGee said.
While McGee doubted the BOJ has a particular exchange rate in mind, he said the BOJ does not want to see the yen tumble over a short period of time.
"I think that's partly because it's hard to get foreign investors to stay in the Japanese stock market if they're seeing the value of the yen continually decline," McGee said.
